key_finding: A nudge that shrouded the credit-card minimum-payment autopay option cut minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce debt, partly because it also reduced autopay enrollment and increased missed payments.
methodology: Field experiment on real credit-card accounts with six-month follow-up.
why_it_matters: Directly tests the brief's central worry: a choice-architecture change can move the enrollment/behavior number without moving the outcome that matters, and can create new harm (missed payments) for liquidity-constrained users — the clearest self-directed consumer-financial analogue we have.
limitations: credit-card debt repayment, not a savings feature
shrouding a default is a stronger intervention than the opt-in/opt-out/active-choice menu under consideration
relevance_reason: Shows a default/nudge changing nominal enrollment behavior while failing to change the substantive financial outcome, in a genuinely consumer self-directed financial product.

key_finding: Synthesizes the DC-plan literature on how automatic enrollment and default investment options affect participation and contribution rates short- and long-term, including negative effects on participant engagement.
methodology: Narrative state-of-the-art review of academic and industry literature. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Useful map of what the employer-pension literature already found and disputes, so the team knows which claims are settled versus contested before assuming they transfer to a consumer app.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan setting, not a consumer app
narrative overview, not a systematic review with pooled effect sizes
relevance_reason: Comprehensive recent overview of default effects in the analogous but distinct employer-retirement literature the brief flags as needing careful translation.

key_finding: Default enrollment raises short-term participation and coverage but induces long-term passivity — low contribution rates, inattentive accounts, and account churn — such that participation alone does not demonstrate welfare improvement.
methodology: Narrative policy/welfare discussion drawing on empirical retirement-savings literature. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: States explicitly the 'vanity enrollment' concern the support team raises, and proposes mitigations (auto-escalation, re-enrollment reminders) worth considering if opt-out is chosen.
limitations: U.S. retirement plan context, not liquid consumer savings
no quantitative effect sizes given in the abstract
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that default enrollment alone is a welfare win, matching the support team's objection.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework for when default effects persist or fade downstream, driven by the time course of choice/consumption, prior preferences, and salience of trade-offs.
methodology: Conceptual synthesis and framework-building across the consumer-defaults literature. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives the team a structured way to predict and measure whether the round-up default's effect on enrollment will persist or decay by 6-12 months, and what moderators (salience, prior intent) to watch for.
limitations: theoretical/synthesis paper, no new effect-size estimates
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: General consumer-behavior review addressing exactly the persistence-of-defaults question the brief asks about, in a non-employer setting.

key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive even when the default is a poor fit, with active-choice variation driven by transitory shocks rather than attentiveness.
methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default options in a large administrative dataset.
why_it_matters: Strong evidence that defaults can persist regardless of value-mismatch and that heterogeneity in 'who opts out' is largely random rather than driven by informed choice — a caution against assuming active choosers are the engaged ones.
limitations: health-insurance enrollment, not a consumer financial product
low-income Medicare population differs from a mobile banking app's user base
relevance_reason: Rigorous natural-experiment evidence on default persistence and insensitivity to option value, directly bearing on distributional/manipulation-risk questions even though the setting differs.

key_finding: Steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from automatic enrollment and 0.3% from default auto-escalation once job turnover, balance withdrawal at separation, and opt-out from escalation are accounted for; only 40% of auto-escalated employees escalate on the first date.
methodology: Longitudinal administrative analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating job separation and withdrawal dynamics.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of the support team's objection: default-driven enrollment gains are much smaller in steady state than the headline participation-rate effect suggests.
limitations: retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings
employer-plan turnover dynamics (vesting, job separation) don't map onto a banking app
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that defaults durably raise saving amounts, using the most rigorous long-run design available.

key_finding: Nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income German employees raised pension participation by 23 percentage points, but most affected individuals actively opted out, with the default effect strongest when incentives are high and enrollment status is poorly understood.
methodology: Natural experiment using linked administrative and survey data around a nationwide policy introduction.
why_it_matters: Shows the default effect's size is conditional on incentive salience and ease of opting out — informs how strong an opt-out effect to expect if the round-up feature's benefit is not obviously salient.
limitations: public pension system, not a consumer app
opt-out behavior driven by knowledge of enrollment status, a different information environment than an app onboarding flow
relevance_reason: Quantifies default effect size and its moderators (incentive salience, knowledge of status), directly informing when to expect a strong versus weak opt-out effect.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's participation and contribution gains, replicated at 12 months, attenuate substantially by 36 months, though the policy still meaningfully reduces savings inequality; a life-cycle model fits the pattern with a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Analysis of over 100 US retirement plans plus a UK representative panel, combined with a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Direct evidence that default effects on enrollment fade with horizon even as distributional benefits (reduced inequality) can persist — a nuanced version of the support team's concern that's worth separating from a pure 'defaults don't work' claim.
limitations: retirement savings rather than liquid short-term savings
structural model estimates are model-dependent
relevance_reason: Gives a 12-vs-36-month comparison of default persistence with a quantified switching cost, the exact horizon question the brief asks about.

key_finding: Across three experiments including a 4,207-person study spanning five European countries, defaults produced medium-to-large effects on risk-taking, but also lowered ratings of the advisor's advice, especially when the targeted default was refused — with framing of the default question shifting outcomes by smaller amounts.
methodology: Three experiments, including a large representative multi-country European sample, on financial risk-taking decisions with wealth-manager defaults.
why_it_matters: Directly answers the EU dark-pattern question in the brief: defaults move behavior but can damage perceived trustworthiness of the institution, especially when a poorly-fitted default is refused — a real reputational-risk signal for choosing opt-out enrollment or a mismatched preset multiplier.
limitations: single-session experimental measure, no 6-12 month persistence data
wealth-management risk allocation rather than round-up savings specifically
relevance_reason: EU-based, consumer self-directed financial-decision evidence on when a default reads as helpful versus manipulative, directly informing the reputational-risk constraint in the brief.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85% at three firms, but about 80% of participants initially accepted both the low default savings rate and conservative default fund, with half still at the default rate/fund after three years.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms tracking 401(k) participation and contribution behavior over multiple years.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that presetting a specific level anchors most users there for years — the founding evidence for the brief's C3 anchoring concern about which round-up multiplier to pre-select.
limitations: undated/older employer 401(k) study, superseded in relevance by more recent work per the brief's own framing
retirement plan setting, not liquid consumer savings
relevance_reason: The foundational study establishing that preset default levels anchor most participants for years, which the newer literature the brief wants argues with.

key_finding: Structural analysis of 8.6 million tipping decisions finds 84% of default adherence comes from the interaction of deviation cost and opt-out cost together; adding a lower option to a fixed default menu (a 15% tip below 20/25/30%) captures 69% of achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on transaction data, validated against an independent stated-preference survey.
why_it_matters: Gives a transferable method and finding for the level-preset decision: a menu of preset multipliers with one selected functions like the tip-menu structure studied here, and shows how adding/adjusting the menu of preset options shifts welfare and adherence — directly informs whether to add a lower multiplier option and where to anchor it.
limitations: taxi tipping, not a savings product
consumer preferences for tipping norms may not generalize to savings-rate preferences
relevance_reason: Provides a directly transferable structural-model method for reasoning about preset-menu design (which default to pick, what happens if you add another option) — the mechanism explicitly named as analogous to the round-up multiplier decision.

key_finding: An opt-in payroll-deduction short-term savings program at five UK firms saw very low take-up (under 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated), but among those who did, 96% still held a balance and 87% received an automatic contribution at 12 months.
methodology: Field study of a new choice-architecture product launch across five UK employers, tracking account activation and 12-month balances/contributions.
why_it_matters: Directly relevant to the product type (short-term, liquid, withdrawable savings, unlike a pension): shows opt-in alone yields very low reach but the enrolled minority stays highly engaged for a year — useful evidence that opt-in quality of engagement can be high even if headline numbers are low.
limitations: employer payroll-deduction channel, not a self-directed banking app onboarding flow
no comparison to opt-out or active-choice enrollment in this program
relevance_reason: Closest available product analogue (short-term, liquid savings) to the round-up feature, showing opt-in take-up and 12-month persistence numbers.

key_finding: Characterizes when opt-out-minimizing versus opt-out-maximizing defaults are asymptotically optimal, depending on whether the designer and choosers agree on the activity's value, with extensions to externalities and normative ambiguity.
methodology: Theoretical/normative economic model with numerical simulations validating asymptotic approximations.
why_it_matters: Offers a normative frame for deciding what an 'optimal' default looks like when the bank's and the user's interests may not fully align — relevant to whether an opt-out default is defensible as helpful rather than self-serving.
limitations: purely theoretical with no empirical grounding in a financial-product setting
abstract gives no concrete numeric guidance for a specific default choice
relevance_reason: General welfare-theoretic framework for evaluating whether an opt-out default is justifiable, relevant to the manipulation-risk question even without empirical estimates.

key_finding: Maps EU laws on dark patterns and proposes a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations to distinguish acceptable defaults from manipulative choice architecture.
methodology: Legal/doctrinal analysis and taxonomy development; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete EU-law framework for judging whether an opt-out or pre-selected default counts as an autonomy-violating dark pattern, directly informing the entry-design decision's reputational/legal risk.
limitations: Legal/normative analysis, no empirical effect-size data
Not specific to financial products or savings apps
relevance_reason: Directly addresses the EU dark-pattern risk the brief flags as a reputational concern for defaulting users into the feature.

key_finding: With a 12% default contribution rate, only 25% of employees had opted out after 12 months (versus roughly half in plans with lower defaults), and low-income employees were disproportionately likely to remain stuck at a default that was suboptimal for their income level.
methodology: Empirical analysis of employer retirement plan enrollment data with an unusually high default; literature-review comparison.
why_it_matters: Shows a preset level can anchor low-income users onto a suboptimal contribution rate, a caution against a high preset multiplier without regard to income heterogeneity in the round-up feature.
limitations: Employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a self-directed consumer product
No employer-as-intermediary equivalent exists in a banking app
relevance_reason: Closest pension-literature analogue to the level/default-multiplier anchoring question, with distributional effects by income.

key_finding: Abstract not available; title indicates field experiments on automating short-term payroll savings in the UK.
methodology: abstract-only
why_it_matters: Potentially relevant to short-term, liquid automated savings design, but no usable evidence content is available to assess design impact.
limitations: Abstract missing/truncated, no extractable findings
Payroll-linked mechanism differs from card-based round-up saving in a banking app
relevance_reason: Title suggests direct relevance to short-term automated savings design but the abstract provides no substantive content to evaluate.

key_finding: Automatic (opt-out) enrollment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts at UK banks reduced unarranged overdraft charges by 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges by 4-8%, implying £170-240 million in market-wide annual savings, though alerts captured less than half of consumers' potential savings.
methodology: At-scale field experiments at major UK banks.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates that opt-out default enrollment into a protective banking feature produces large, real, at-scale behavioral effects in the same UK consumer-banking context as our app, directly supporting opt-out as a viable entry design.
limitations: Feature is a warning alert rather than a savings-contribution decision with a preset level
Does not report 6-12 month persistence, withdrawal, or complaint outcomes
relevance_reason: Closest real-world consumer-banking analogue to opt-out enrollment into a beneficial feature, quantifying the scale of the default effect.

key_finding: Automatic pension enrollment increased savings but was partially offset by increased unsecured debt (about £7 in debt per £32-38 in extra pension savings) over 41 months, with modest increases in mortgage uptake and balances.
methodology: Large-scale natural experiment from the UK auto-enrollment pension roll-out across roughly 160,000 employers.
why_it_matters: Shows a default-driven rise in nominal savings is not a clean welfare win because it can be substantially offset by debt, warning against treating enrolment or pot growth as proof of benefit for round-up savers.
limitations: Retirement pension context, not liquid consumer savings
Employer-mediated auto-enrollment with no direct employer-analogue in our app
relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that default enrollment straightforwardly benefits savers, directly bearing on the amount-saved-vs-nominal-enrollment question.

key_finding: Adding a minor enrollment 'ordeal' (removing auto-enrollment) reduced health insurance enrollment by 33% and differentially excluded young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people.
methodology: Natural experiment studying removal of an auto-enrollment policy for health insurance.
why_it_matters: Shows that removing a default can disproportionately exclude vulnerable, less-engaged users, informing the brief's question of who is helped and who is hurt by opt-in versus opt-out design.
limitations: Health insurance selection market with adverse-selection dynamics absent from a savings product
Not a financial-savings or fintech setting
relevance_reason: Provides distributional evidence on who is excluded when a default is removed, directly speaking to the brief's who-is-helped-who-is-hurt question.

key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults on political campaign websites increased donations by over $43 million but also increased refund requests by almost $3 million, with larger effects on smaller and less-experienced donors who did not compensate by changing donation amounts.
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design across campaign websites' default rollout timing, 2020 US election.
why_it_matters: A rare study of a recurring-financial-commitment default in a self-directed consumer setting, showing such defaults disproportionately affect naive and small users and generate regret (refunds) — directly relevant to the dark-pattern and vulnerable-user risk of defaulting people into ongoing round-up saving.
limitations: Political donations, not a savings or banking product
US setting rather than EU consumer-protection regulatory context
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the simple defaults-always-help premise by documenting donor regret/refunds and disproportionate impact on inexperienced, small contributors from a recurring financial default.

key_finding: A default option raises the reservation utility via a reference effect, leading to better choices, and higher-reservation-utility individuals self-select into active search and are more likely to find superior options.
methodology: Behavioral/experimental economics lab study with a formal search-and-default model.
why_it_matters: Offers a theoretical mechanism for why users who reject a default end up better off, relevant to thinking about heterogeneity in who benefits from opting out, but not tied to a savings or financial-app context.
limitations: Abstract gives no domain specifics tying it to financial products
Generic lab search-choice experiment, not enrollment or contribution decisions
relevance_reason: Provides a general mechanism for default-driven self-selection that could explain heterogeneous benefit, but is not situated in the project's setting.

key_finding: Following the EU Digital Markets Act's mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage rose 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual from 15 months post-rollout onward, with differences tied to rollout scope.
methodology: Difference-in-differences analysis around the EU DMA choice-screen rollout on iOS and Android.
why_it_matters: Direct, large-scale, real-world evidence that mandatory active choice screens in mobile apps under EU regulation substantially shift outcomes away from incumbent defaults, strong evidence for how much benefit active choice could capture versus opt-out.
limitations: Browser choice, not a financial-savings decision
Does not measure engagement or persistence of the choice made, only usage share
relevance_reason: The clearest EU regulatory precedent quantifying forced active choice against incumbent defaults in a mobile-app context, central to the entry-design decision.

key_finding: A usability study of nine opt-out interface designs for Global Privacy Control found that more 'generalizable' active-choice schemes reduced disruption (98% not disrupted for the best scheme, a 40-point improvement over baseline) with only a slight loss of choice-level utility.
methodology: Usability study with 410 participants testing browser-extension privacy choice interfaces.
why_it_matters: Offers interface-design techniques for making active/opt-out choice less disruptive and more usable, potentially informing how an active-choice onboarding screen could be designed to reduce friction, but drawn from privacy law rather than financial products.
limitations: Domain is privacy consent, not financial savings enrollment
No enrollment-rate or savings-amount outcome is measured
relevance_reason: Offers UX-design lessons for reducing friction in active-choice interfaces, tangential to but not directly answering the enrolment-design question.

key_finding: An opt-out default for university exam sign-up increased sign-up uptake, but increased actual exam completion and passing only for a single exam with stronger endorsement, and only among students who had previously been responsive to university communication; non-responsive students showed increased sign-ups but no effect on outcomes.
methodology: Two field experiments changing exam sign-up procedures to opt-out.
why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates the core disengagement risk the brief worries about: a default can inflate nominal enrollment without changing effortful outcomes for people who wouldn't have engaged anyway, matching the support team's vanity-metric concern.
limitations: University exam context, not a financial savings product
Small institutional sample, not a consumer banking population
relevance_reason: Empirically shows defaults can raise headline enrollment without changing effortful outcomes for disengaged users, matching the project's central engagement-vs-vanity-enrollment concern.

key_finding: After target-date funds became a default investment option under the Pension Protection Act, portfolio stock-share allocation became more age-dependent, but contribution rates changed little.
methodology: Account-level panel data on millions of US middle-class retirement investors, 2006-2018.
why_it_matters: Shows a default can strongly reshape one dimension of behavior (asset allocation) while leaving contribution levels largely unaffected, cautioning against assuming a preset multiplier will move contribution levels much.
limitations: Employer-sponsored retirement investment context, not consumer savings enrollment
Studies an asset-allocation default rather than an enrollment or contribution-level default
relevance_reason: Illustrates that defaults can be inert for contribution-level decisions even while powerfully steering another default-linked dimension, relevant to the anchoring question.

key_finding: In an RCT of behavioral nudges for voluntary pension saving in China, all tested nudges — including default options — significantly reduced willingness to contribute relative to control, with heterogeneous backfire effects by income, education, and gender.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey, n=220.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the brief's working assumption that defaults reliably raise participation, showing default-option nudges can backfire and reduce contribution willingness for specific demographic segments — a strong caution before defaulting everyone in.
limitations: Voluntary pension saving survey in China, cultural/institutional context differs from EU consumer banking
Small sample (n=220) and stated intent rather than observed behavior
relevance_reason: One of the few studies here finding default options backfire rather than help, directly answering the brief's request for evidence contradicting the defaults-always-help premise.

key_finding: Across 36 hypothetical financial-intervention scenarios with 2,100 Australians, people rate interventions positively overall, strongly prefer System-2 (reflective) framings and saving-framed messages, and transparency has no significant effect on approval or perceived manipulation.
methodology: Pre-registered vignette survey experiment, representative Australian sample, 2x2x2-style manipulation of transparency, framing, and System 1/2 targeting.
why_it_matters: Directly informs how to frame the round-up default and multiplier copy to avoid a dark-pattern read: saving-framed, System-2-style prompts are best received, and disclosure of mechanism does not hurt approval, which de-risks an opt-out design if messaged this way.
limitations: hypothetical scenarios, not a live product with real money at stake
measures stated approval, not actual enrollment or savings behaviour
relevance_reason: Speaks directly to the EU dark-pattern/manipulation-perception risk named in the brief for choosing between opt-out framings.

key_finding: Offering CCT beneficiaries a bank-account payment channel had no significant average effect on savings or downstream outcomes, but raised balances specifically among those with nonpositive prior balances.
methodology: Field experiment comparing cash vs. bank-account delivery of conditional cash transfers, abstract-only detail.
why_it_matters: Suggests that access/channel changes alone (analogous to enrolling people into a savings vehicle) mainly help those who previously saved nothing, echoing the brief's concern about who a default actually helps.
limitations: developing-country CCT population, not a fintech consumer product
not about opt-in/opt-out/active-choice enrolment design at all
relevance_reason: Tangential evidence on channel/access effects on savings, useful only as weak distributional analogy.

key_finding: Abstract is truncated/garbled, noting only that contribution amounts and liquid-fund program benefits are identical across compared cases.
methodology: abstract-only; appears to compare automatic-IRA program variants with an emergency-savings feature.
why_it_matters: Potentially relevant to liquid-savings-plus-retirement design but the abstract gives no usable effect size or design detail to act on.
limitations: abstract too fragmentary to extract findings
auto-IRA is a policy-mandated retirement vehicle, not a self-directed consumer app
relevance_reason: Topically adjacent (automatic enrolment plus liquid savings) but too uninformative to be actionable.

key_finding: Switching a 401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrollment dramatically raised participation, and most auto-enrolled employees stuck to the default contribution rate and default fund allocation rather than choosing their own.
methodology: Before/after natural experiment using administrative data from one large U.S. corporation's 401(k) plan.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that a preset default doesn't just enroll people, it anchors their contribution level too — directly relevant to whether a preset multiplier (1x/2x/5x) will anchor users away from their true preference.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan where the employer is a trusted intermediary, a mechanism the brief says does not carry over
no measure of engagement, withdrawal, or amount saved beyond default acceptance
relevance_reason: Foundational study the newer default-effect literature responds to; establishes the anchoring mechanism the brief asks about for preset levels.

key_finding: No abstract available; title indicates a comparison of savings behaviours between automatic and voluntary enrollment in a defined-contribution retirement plan.
methodology: abstract-only, presumably observational comparison of enrollment types.
why_it_matters: Could bear on persistence of default effects but with no abstract there is nothing concrete to act on.
limitations: no abstract provided, so findings and effect sizes are unknown
employer/DC retirement plan setting rather than consumer app
relevance_reason: On-topic title but unusable without any content beyond the title.

key_finding: Institutional mistrust and minority status independently predict both under-saving and early withdrawal of retirement savings, suggesting the same vulnerable groups are hurt on both sides of the saving decision.
methodology: Analysis of three representative Estonian surveys (2020-2022) around a pension early-withdrawal policy reform.
why_it_matters: Directly supports the brief's concern about distributional harm: the people most likely to disengage or withdraw after being passively enrolled may be exactly those with low institutional trust, which argues against a blanket opt-out.
limitations: mandatory pension scheme context, not a liquid consumer round-up product
withdrawal behaviour studied is a policy-driven lump-sum option, not routine app disengagement
relevance_reason: Gives concrete distributional evidence — who is hurt by low engagement/early withdrawal — that speaks to the brief's C5 concern.

key_finding: In a 24,303-respondent G7 survey experiment, prompting people to reflect on an automatic-enrollment default for vaccine boosters reduced stated intentions to comply and reduced approval of the policy.
methodology: Large-scale online survey experiment across G7 countries with random assignment to reflection/control conditions.
why_it_matters: Directly challenges the 'defaults always help, and are received neutrally' premise: making a default salient can trigger backlash, which is exactly the reputational risk the brief flags for an opt-out design in a regulatory-sensitive EU market.
limitations: health/vaccination domain, not a financial product
measures stated intentions and approval, not actual enrollment behaviour
relevance_reason: Best available evidence that reflecting on/disclosing a default can backfire, contradicting the brief's default-optimism premise, though drawn from a non-financial domain.

key_finding: Among Millennials, automatic enrollment and employer contributions are associated with higher likelihood of retirement plan participation, while their absence explains much of non-participation.
methodology: Cross-sectional analysis of the 2018 FINRA Millennial Investment Study survey data.
why_it_matters: Reconfirms the auto-enrollment participation lift already well established elsewhere, adding little new beyond what Madrian/Choi et al. show, and in the employer-plan setting the brief says doesn't transfer.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan with employer as intermediary, the mechanism the brief excludes
cross-sectional/observational, no causal identification of the enrollment design effect
relevance_reason: Same-question replication in the excluded employer-retirement setting, offering little beyond already-established literature.

key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, each $1 of subsidy spending raises saving by only 1 cent for the ~15% of 'active' (wealthier, sophisticated) savers, while automatic employer contributions substantially raise saving for the ~85% of 'passive' savers who are unresponsive to subsidies.
methodology: Large-scale administrative panel data analysis of Danish retirement savings accounts, decomposing active vs. passive saver responses.
why_it_matters: The clearest large-sample evidence that passive/default mechanisms work precisely because most people don't respond to active incentives — and that the people helped by defaults are the least financially sophisticated, a distributional pattern the brief explicitly asks to check before defaulting everyone in.
limitations: Danish retirement savings accounts with employer-mediated automatic contributions, not a liquid consumer app
does not measure engagement, withdrawal, or satisfaction, only balances
relevance_reason: Foundational, very large-sample evidence on exactly the who-benefits-from-defaults question, despite being in the excluded employer-pension setting.

key_finding: Field experiments show 'active choice' (forcing a yes/no decision with no default) and an 'enhanced active choice' variant (highlighting losses from the non-preferred option) can motivate behavior change, including savings behavior, as an alternative or complement to automatic enrollment.
methodology: Literature review plus a series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice designs.
why_it_matters: This is the paper that directly tests the third enrolment option the brief is deciding between — active choice — and proposes a concrete enhanced variant, giving a design alternative to opt-out that avoids the ethical/manipulation concerns of automatic enrollment.
limitations: field experiments span health (medication adherence) and savings domains, not specifically a consumer fintech app
abstract does not report enrolment or persistence effect sizes
relevance_reason: Directly addresses C6, the active-choice-vs-default comparison at the heart of the entry-design decision.

key_finding: This overview of behavioral household finance synthesizes evidence on consumption/savings, borrowing, payments, and asset allocation, and reviews interventions including choice architecture and product design that firms and governments use to shape household financial behavior.
methodology: Narrative literature review/book chapter (NBER), abstract-only detail on specific effect sizes.
why_it_matters: The closest available synthesis on consumer (not employer-mediated) financial choice architecture, giving a framework for weighing defaults, active choice, and product design against the brief's two open decisions.
limitations: a narrative synthesis, not a quantitative meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes
abstract does not specify household-finance-specific default effect magnitudes
relevance_reason: The review-type synthesis the brief asks for, in the consumer/household finance setting closest to the product being built.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85% at three firms, but about 80% of participants initially accepted both the low default contribution rate and conservative default fund, and half still did so after three years, roughly offsetting the participation gains in terms of total accumulation.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large firms with automatic 401(k) enrollment.
why_it_matters: The single clearest evidence that a default raises headline enrolment while anchoring most people at the preset level for years — precisely the 'nominal enrolment vs. real saving' distinction the brief needs resolved before picking a preset multiplier.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k), not a liquid consumer product, and the employer-as-intermediary mechanism the brief excludes
does not measure withdrawal, disengagement, or complaint behaviour
relevance_reason: Foundational quantitative evidence on both persistence (C2) and anchoring (C3), the two hardest-to-find effect sizes for this decision.

key_finding: In a randomized field experiment in Afghanistan, default enrollment into a salary-linked savings account raised participation by 40 percentage points (equivalent to a 50% match), driven mainly by present bias and the cognitive cost of evaluating savings scenarios, and also increased later active saving.
methodology: Randomized field experiment varying salary-linked savings account defaults among employees, with follow-up interventions to isolate mechanisms.
why_it_matters: Offers a causal mechanism for why defaults work (cognitive cost, present bias) that predicts whether an active-choice design would recover most of the benefit without the cost — relevant to the brief's active-choice question even though not in a fintech app.
limitations: salary-linked employer-facilitated savings account in a developing-country context, not an EU consumer banking app
does not report enrolment persistence or withdrawal at 6-12 months
relevance_reason: Best mechanism-level evidence on why defaults move behaviour, useful for predicting whether active choice can substitute for a full opt-out default.

key_finding: Payment reminders reduced credit card late-payment fees by 14% but increased overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while other users saved 15%.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil, studying direct and indirect effects of nudging on fee outcomes.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the brief's concern about who is helped and who is hurt: a well-intentioned nudge in a consumer fintech setting produced a subgroup that was made worse off, which is exactly the distributional risk the round-up enrolment decision needs to guard against before defaulting everyone in.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrolment defaults or contribution-level anchoring
Brazilian credit/overdraft context rather than EU round-up savings
no measurement of persistence at 6-12 months, only aggregate fee outcomes
no active-choice comparison arm
relevance_reason: Strong evidence on heterogeneous/distributional effects of a financial nudge and a clear contradiction of the 'nudges/defaults always help' premise, in a self-directed consumer financial app setting.
